summary: This Best Current Practice describes an architecture for location information in Internet applications, including privacy. It covers how to gather and transfer location securely while protecting individuals, with rules attached to the data.

eli5.summary: Apps need to know where you are but you should control who learns it. This describes a system with rules that travel with your location.

questions: how does location privacy work on the internet
subtitle: How location data can travel across the Internet with the owner's privacy rules attached to it.

tldr.problem: Location-based services need to gather and pass on where people and devices are, but location data is unusually sensitive and users normally cannot say how recipients may use it.
tldr.mechanism: The Geopriv architecture defines roles (Target, Device, Rule Maker, Location Generator, Location Server, Location Recipient) and a Location Object that always carries Privacy Rules, which are default-deny grants of permission. Security requirements cover each phase of the location life cycle: positioning, distribution and use.
tldr.outcome: Recipients know what they are allowed to do, so those who misuse location data do so knowingly. The RFC is clear that Geopriv cannot technically guarantee that rules are honored. It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 3693 and RFC 3694.

today: RFC 6280 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 160) from July 2011 that updates RFC 3693 and RFC 3694. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Location Needs Special Care
sections.content:
Navigation, emergency services, friend finders and equipment tracking all need the geographic location of hosts, users and other entities. RFC 6280 describes the Geopriv architecture, whose central piece is the location object. It carries location information about an individual or device together with user-specified privacy rules. It also revises and expands the earlier Geopriv requirements (RFC 3693 and RFC 3694) and is meant as a good first document for readers new to Geopriv.

Location is risky because it is often produced on mobile devices, so it can be collected everywhere, any time, often without user interaction. It can reveal that someone was at a particular medical clinic at a particular time. The RFC also names risks of stalking and domestic violence, and notes that governments take an interest in location data, while laws on how they may obtain it are in some places non-existent or out of date.
sections.eli5: Where you are says a lot about you, like which doctor you visited. So the places you go should be shared only with people you pick.

sections.title: Binding Rules to the Data
sections.content:
Traditionally, recipients of data decide how it is used, and users face a binary choice: share or not. Geopriv shifts this so that the person the data is about states their own preferences. Rules can be simple ("do not share my location with others") or richer, such as letting a spouse always see an exact location but a boss only during work hours.

The RFC compares this to Creative Commons licences and document classification markings: rules travel with the thing they govern, so every recipient knows the terms. Because of this, no recipient can disavow knowledge of the user's preferences.

Geopriv does not, by itself, give a technical way to guarantee that rules are honored. Its protection comes largely from recipients being informed of the rules and expected to follow them. Having the rules attached also helps legal contracts, consumer protection authorities and marketplace feedback to enforce them.
sections.eli5: Like a library book with a due date stamped inside: whoever borrows it can see the rules. It does not stop a rule-breaker, but they cannot say they did not know.

sections.title: Roles and Data Formats
sections.content:
The architecture has two privacy goals: location goes only to authorized entities, and those entities are told how they may use it. Rules come in two classes: access control rules (who may receive location, and in what form) and usage rules (what uses are authorized).

Six roles take part:

  • Target: the person or object whose location is sought and whose privacy is protected.
  • Device: the phone, PC or microcontroller tracked as a proxy for the Target.
  • Rule Maker (RM): creates the rules for a Target. It may be the Target, a parent, or a corporate security officer.
  • Location Generator (LG): works out the Device's location, for example a GPS chip or a cellular network.
  • Location Server (LS): takes in location and rules, applies the rules and passes location on. A presence server or a browser can be an LS.
  • Location Recipient (LR): receives location information.

One entity can play several roles. The two data formats are the Location Object (geodetic data such as latitude and longitude, or civic data such as street and city, bundled with Privacy Rules) and the Privacy Rule itself.
sections.eli5: Think of passing a note in class. One kid finds the secret, a messenger decides who may see it, the friends read it, and the note carries the owner's rules.

sections.title: The Location Life Cycle
sections.content:
Location moves through three phases: positioning (an LG determines the Device's location), distribution (LSes send it to LRs, which may become LSes and pass it on) and use (an LR receives and uses it).

Positioning can be device-based (manual entry or unassisted satellite positioning), network-based (an external LG such as an ISP knows enough about the Device, as in wiremap-based location) or network-assisted (the Device sends measurements or the LG sends assistance data). For privacy, local identifiers, unlinked pseudonyms or private identifiers should be used when possible. An LG that is not privacy-aware must hand location only to a small fixed set of LSes. Protocols for positioning MUST provide confidentiality and integrity protection.

Distribution is where rules matter most. Rules are default-deny: an empty rule set means all requests are denied except those from the Target itself, and every rule is a positive grant of permission. An LS enforces rules by denying requests or by transforming the location, for example sending only city and country. Local Rules stay inside the LS. Forwarded Rules travel inside the Location Object, and only the minimal subset needed is sent, because rules can themselves reveal sensitive information. Location Objects carry a limited set of Forwarded Rules covering Retention and Retransmission, with an option to point to more robust external rules.

A Location Configuration Protocol lets a Device learn its own location from a Location Information Server (LIS). An LS with no rules for a Target MUST follow the "LCP policy": give location only to the Target. Location can also be passed by reference as a URI, which lets the LS apply access control to each recipient. If the URI has no access control, it needs a random component with enough entropy to make guessing infeasible.

Use is simple for a recipient that does not retransmit or retain the location beyond the interaction: it complies with any rule set. A recipient that wants to retain or retransmit MUST examine the rules, and any usage MUST be explicitly authorized.
sections.eli5: A secret goes on a trip: someone finds it, messengers carry it, and someone finally uses it. Each stop has its own rulebook, and anything not allowed counts as not allowed.

sections.title: Combining Rules and Securing Distribution
sections.content:
An LS MUST accept rules only from authorized Rule Makers. If an LS receives no rules with a Location Object, it MUST delete it. If the Location Object has no rule allowing retransmission, the LS MUST NOT transmit it. When an LS has rules both from Rule Makers and inside the Location Object, how to combine them is local policy. The RFC lists four example policies: Union, Intersection, RM Override and LO Override. Union is the default, following RFC 4745. Intersection is the most privacy-protective, and it is RECOMMENDED that an LS lets Rule Makers find out which policy applies.

For security, protocols carrying Location Objects or rules MUST allow mutual authentication and MUST provide integrity protection. Location Objects SHOULD be transmitted with end-to-end confidentiality. Where protocols protect messages only hop by hop, it is RECOMMENDED that the protocol allow encrypted Location Objects or a reference instead.
sections.eli5: If two grown-ups give different rules for the same toy, the house has to pick a way to combine them. The strictest way is safest for the kid whose toy it is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A protocol can protect only one hop at a time, for example with IPsec or TLS. Across several hops, entities get assurances only if every segment is mutually authenticated and each entity talks only to those it trusts. Sending a URI instead of the object effectively turns a multi-hop path into a single hop: the dereference between the recipient and the server.

A Location Object binds four things together: Target identifiers, location, timestamps and rules. Each party needs assurances about these bindings. The Rule Maker needs its rules correctly tied to the Target. The Location Server needs authentic rules and must authenticate Rule Makers to prevent rule tampering. The Location Recipient needs authentic location, identity and time, to prevent falsified locations, modified timestamps, faked identities and replayed objects. The Location Generator needs to publish only to a Location Server it trusts.

Protection can also be built into the object itself. RFC 4119 describes using S/MIME for integrity and confidentiality. This is not always practical, for example when there is no direct trust between creator and recipient or many recipients are authorized.
sections.eli5: A lock on one door does not protect the whole hallway. Sending just a ticket number that must be exchanged at one desk means there is only one door to guard.

sections.title: Worked Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC walks through four examples. In the minimal scenario, a Device finds its own location and sends it to get a service, for instance in an HTTP POST or a SIP INVITE. The server neither retains nor retransmits it, so it need not even read the rules.

In location-based web services, a browser asks the user for permission, builds a Location Object with the user's rules and hands it to the page. Sending it to a back-end server is internal to the recipient, but passing it to a third-party map site would require checking the rules.

In emergency calling, the caller's location goes to a mapping server through LoST and then to the Public Safety Answering Point in a SIP INVITE. The LoST server may use location only to complete the protocol. Depending on regulation, the answering point may ignore the rules or be bound by them.

In the combination of services example, Alice's location flows from her ISP to a presence service, then Bob, a photo site and Eve. Eve ignores the rules, but a social networking site checks them and rejects the upload because they do not allow retransmission or retention.
sections.eli5: The examples show the rules working in real life, from a map app that forgets your spot right away to a website that refuses a post because the sticky-note rules say no.
